body:
Why surface area alone cannot explain every nanoscale property

A larger surface-area-to-volume ratio explains why small particles may interact more strongly with surrounding substances. However, it does not fully explain why some nanoscale particles emit different colours of light or exhibit unusual electrical behaviour.

These changes can arise because electrons behave differently when the available space becomes extremely small.

In ordinary bulk materials, very large numbers of atoms combine to produce electronic properties characteristic of the material. When a material is confined to a sufficiently small region, the available electronic energy states may change.

This behaviour is described using quantum physics, but its basic consequences can be understood without mathematical calculations.

What is quantum confinement?

Quantum confinement

Quantum confinement occurs when the motion of electrons and related electronic excitations is restricted by the very small dimensions of a material. This restriction can change the electronic energy states and therefore influence the material's optical or electrical properties.

Quantum confinement is particularly important in certain semiconductor nanocrystals. A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a typical conductor and a typical insulator and can be controlled by factors such as composition, temperature or added impurities.

In sufficiently small semiconductor particles, changing the particle size can change the energy required for electronic transitions. As a result, particles made from the same semiconductor may absorb or emit light of different wavelengths.

Quantum dots and size-dependent colour

A quantum dot is a nanoscale structure in which electrons and related electronic excitations are confined in a very small region. Semiconductor quantum dots are especially well known for their size-dependent optical properties.

For quantum dots of the same semiconductor composition, within the range where quantum confinement is important:

  • Smaller quantum dots generally have larger electronic energy gaps and emit shorter-wavelength light.
  • Larger quantum dots generally have smaller electronic energy gaps and emit longer-wavelength light.

Within the visible spectrum, shorter wavelengths correspond to the blue side, whereas longer wavelengths correspond to the red side. Thus, changing the size of a suitable quantum dot can change its emitted colour.

The comparison assumes similar composition and suitable excitation conditions. Different semiconductor materials have different energy gaps, so particle size alone cannot predict the exact colour of every quantum dot.

Quantum dots are used in certain modern display technologies to produce selected colours of light. Their use illustrates how controlling nanoscale dimensions can give a material a useful optical property.

Why does nanoscale gold sometimes appear red or purple?

A piece of ordinary bulk gold has the familiar yellow metallic appearance. However, suitably prepared gold nanoparticles dispersed in a transparent liquid may produce red or purple colours.

The explanation involves the interaction of light with electrons in the metal nanoparticles. When light strikes a small metal particle, its conduction electrons can respond collectively to the oscillating electric field of the light. At particular wavelengths, this interaction can strongly influence the light absorbed and scattered by the particle.

This phenomenon is associated with localized surface plasmon resonance. For preliminary examination purposes, the essential idea is that gold nanoparticles can interact with visible light differently from bulk gold.

The resulting colour depends on particle size, shape, separation, surrounding medium and how the particles are distributed.

Two different optical mechanisms

Size-dependent light emission from semiconductor quantum dots is a familiar example of quantum confinement. The red or purple appearance of many gold nanoparticle dispersions is mainly associated with the collective response of electrons in the metal particles to light. These examples should not be treated as having exactly the same physical explanation.

Other properties that may change at the nanoscale

Optical behaviour is only one example. Depending on material and structure, nanoscale dimensions can also affect electrical, thermal, magnetic and mechanical behaviour.

1. Electrical properties

Electrical conductivity depends on the movement of charge carriers, such as electrons, through a material. At the nanoscale, electronic structure, particle boundaries and surface interactions may influence how charges move.

Some nanomaterials are excellent conductors, while others behave as semiconductors or insulators. Being nanoscale does not automatically make a substance electrically conductive.

2. Melting and thermal behaviour

Many materials have characteristic melting points in their bulk forms. For some materials, sufficiently small nanoparticles have lower melting temperatures than larger pieces of the same substance. This can occur because surface atoms have a different bonding environment from atoms in the interior.

The effect is material-dependent. It is incorrect to assume that every nanoparticle melts at a lower temperature or that all nanomaterials conduct heat more efficiently.

3. Magnetic properties

Magnetic behaviour depends on the material's electronic structure and how magnetic regions respond to external magnetic fields. When some magnetic materials are divided into sufficiently small particles, their magnetic behaviour can differ from that of their bulk forms.

This principle is useful in selected magnetic storage, sensing and biomedical technologies. However, nanoscale size does not make every material magnetic.

4. Mechanical strength and hardness

The strength and hardness of a solid depend on its bonding, structure and imperfections. Nanostructured materials may exhibit improved hardness, strength or wear resistance when their internal structure is appropriately controlled.

For example, some nanostructured coatings improve resistance to scratching or wear. However, nanoparticles are not necessarily stronger than larger pieces of every material. A useful mechanical property must be established for the particular material and form.

Distinguishing the main causes of property changes

Observed behaviourMain explanationExample
More surface interactionHigher surface-area-to-volume ratioIncreased accessible catalytic surface
Size-dependent light emissionQuantum confinementSemiconductor quantum dots
Different colour of metal nanoparticlesChanged interaction between light and conduction electronsGold nanoparticle dispersions
Changed melting behaviourGreater influence of surface atoms and their bonding environmentSome small metallic nanoparticles
Improved wear resistanceControlled nanoscale structure and material bondingSelected nanostructured coatings

Prelims focus

  • Quantum confinement can alter electronic energy states in sufficiently small structures.
  • For comparable semiconductor quantum dots, smaller dots generally emit shorter-wavelength light than larger dots.
  • Bulk gold appears yellow, while suitable gold nanoparticle dispersions may appear red or purple.
  • Nanoscale dimensions can affect optical, electrical, thermal, magnetic and mechanical properties.
  • Trap: Quantum confinement and increased surface-area-to-volume ratio are different phenomena.
  • Trap: No single electrical, magnetic or melting-point behaviour applies to every nanomaterial.

[Sources: National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'What Is So Special About Nano?', section 'Scale at which quantum effects dominate', accessed 13 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'JILA Solves Problem of Quantum Dot Blinking', published 23 January 2008, updated 3 February 2025; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'Applications of Nanotechnology', sections on electronics, displays and materials, accessed 13 November 2026.]

body:
Nanomaterials are not limited to tiny spherical particles

A nanomaterial can take several forms. Its shape matters because it determines which dimensions are small, how much surface is exposed and how electrons, heat or other substances may interact with the material.

Nanomaterials may be particles, tubes, wires, sheets, coatings or larger solids containing nanoscale internal structures.

Nanoparticles

Nanoparticles have all 3 external dimensions within the nanoscale. They may be approximately spherical, cubic or irregular in shape.

Examples include nanoparticles made from gold, silver, titanium dioxide or zinc oxide. Their properties depend not only on their size but also on their composition, surface and surrounding conditions.

Nanowires and nanotubes

Nanowires are long, thin structures with nanoscale transverse dimensions. Their length may extend beyond the conventional nanoscale range.

A carbon nanotube is a hollow cylindrical structure formed from a network of carbon atoms. Carbon nanotubes can have nanoscale diameters while being much longer than their diameters.

Depending on their atomic structure, carbon nanotubes can have unusual mechanical and electrical properties. They are studied and used in selected reinforced composites, conducting materials and sensors.

Nanosheets and extremely thin films

A nanosheet or thin film may have a very small thickness while its length and width are much larger.

Graphene is a single atomic layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal network. It is an important example of an atomically thin material. Graphene is known for its high mechanical strength and excellent electrical and thermal transport properties under suitable conditions.

Graphene should not be confused with graphite. Ordinary graphite contains many stacked layers of carbon atoms, whereas graphene refers to an individual atomic layer.

Nanostructured bulk materials

A material does not need to be a free nanoparticle to contain nanoscale features. A large object may incorporate nanoscale particles, extremely small internal grains or thin coatings.

For example, a protective coating on a large component may be only nanometres thick. The component itself is not nanoscale, but the coating is a nanoscale structure.

For recognising nanomaterials, examine which dimensions are nanoscale, rather than assuming that every nanomaterial is a tiny sphere. A long nanotube and a wide but atomically thin sheet can both qualify as nanomaterials.

How are nanomaterials produced?

Nanomaterials can be produced through many physical and chemical methods. At the introductory level, the methods are commonly grouped into top-down and bottom-up approaches.

1. Top-down approach

In the top-down approach, the process begins with a larger piece of material and reduces its dimensions or creates progressively smaller features.

Examples include mechanical size reduction and techniques that pattern extremely small structures on a larger surface.

Lithography is a family of patterning techniques used to create small features, particularly in electronics and related manufacturing. Its importance here is that nanoscale patterns can be produced by defining and removing or modifying selected regions of a material.

Mechanical milling can also reduce larger particles into much smaller particles. The exact particle sizes obtained depend on the method and conditions.

2. Bottom-up approach

In the bottom-up approach, materials are built from smaller units such as atoms, molecules or small clusters.

These units combine or arrange themselves to form the desired structures.

Examples include controlled nanoparticle growth, formation of thin films from deposited material and self-assembly, in which suitable building units organise themselves into an ordered arrangement through their interactions.

Some manufacturing methods combine elements of both approaches.

FeatureTop-down approachBottom-up approach
Starting materialLarger solid or structureAtoms, molecules or small building units
Basic principleReduce or pattern existing materialBuild or assemble a structure
Representative methodMilling or lithographyControlled growth or self-assembly
Typical objectiveCreate smaller particles or featuresForm a desired nanoscale structure

How do scientists examine nanoscale structures?

Most nanoscale structures cannot be resolved individually using an ordinary optical microscope. Scientists therefore use instruments with much greater resolving power.

Electron microscopes use electrons to obtain information about very small structures. Scanning probe microscopes examine surfaces using an extremely fine probe.

Such instruments help researchers study nanoparticle shapes, dimensions, surface features and arrangements. The basic distinction is that these are tools for examining nanoscale structures; they are not, by themselves, the definition of nanotechnology.

Why production methods matter for properties

Two samples made from the same chemical substance can behave differently if their particle sizes, shapes or surface conditions are different.

For example, a material formed as separated nanoparticles may expose more surface area than the same material packed into large clusters. Likewise, a thin film may interact with light or electric current differently from an assembly of randomly arranged particles.

The purpose of controlling production is therefore not simply to make a material small. It is to obtain a useful combination of size, structure and properties.

Prelims focus

  • A nanoparticle has all 3 external dimensions in the nanoscale.
  • A nanotube can have nanoscale diameter and much greater length.
  • Graphene is a single atomic layer of carbon arranged in a hexagonal network.
  • Top-down production begins with larger material and reduces or patterns it.
  • Bottom-up production builds structures from smaller units.
  • Trap: Graphene, carbon nanotubes and ordinary graphite are related carbon materials but are not identical structures.

[Sources: National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'Working at the Nanoscale', sections on nanomaterials and nanomanufacturing, accessed 13 November 2026; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'Applications of Nanotechnology', sections on nanomaterials and electronics, accessed 13 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, 'Materials: Metals and Non-metals', printed pp. 44–53, 2018–19 printing, for foundational distinctions between material properties and uses.]
